title: Benefits management: identify to realise
blurb: Explain the five activities of benefits management, build a benefits map, and say what every benefit needs to be realised.
question: A city library service installs self-service kiosks. Six months after go-live, nobody can say whether the promised staff savings have happened, because no one recorded staffing costs beforehand and no one was named to own the saving. What is benefits management, and which parts of it were missed?

teach.h: Managing the value, not just the work
teach.body: Benefits management is the identification, definition, planning, tracking and realisation of benefits. A BENEFIT is a measurable improvement resulting from an outcome that is perceived as an advantage by one or more stakeholders. A DIS-BENEFIT is the opposite: a measurable result perceived as negative. In plain English, benefits management makes sure the organisation actually gets the improvement it invested in, rather than just receiving new things.

teach.h: The five activities of benefits management

steps.label: Identification
steps.sub: What will be better, and for whom?

steps.label: Definition
steps.sub: Make each benefit measurable: measure, baseline, target

steps.label: Planning
steps.sub: Owner, timing, dependencies; how and when realised

steps.label: Tracking
steps.sub: Measure progress and forecasts; act on gaps

steps.label: Realisation
steps.sub: Embed the change so the benefit is achieved

teach.caption: Learn the order exactly: identification, definition, planning, tracking, realisation.

rows.label: What it is
values: The changed situation when it is used

teach.caption: The project delivers outputs. Benefits only appear once those outputs are USED, which is why adoption matters so much.

steps.label: Outcome
steps.sub: Staff spend time on events, not checkouts

steps.label: Benefits
steps.sub: £80k a year saved; 20% more events held

teach.caption: A benefits map links outputs to capabilities and outcomes, outcomes to benefits, and benefits to strategic objectives. Read it right to left to justify the work.

teach.caption: These details often sit in a benefit profile. Miss the baseline and you can't prove the benefit; miss the owner and nobody chases it.

teach.body: Benefits are the reason the business case exists. Without benefits management, a project can deliver every output on time and the organisation can still see no improvement. Defining benefits early keeps scope focused on value; planning gives each one an owner and a date; tracking spots shortfalls while there is still time to act; and realisation activity (training, process change, adoption support) turns new outputs into new results.

teach.h: Benefits arrive late: the extended life cycle
teach.caption: Most benefits are realised after handover, in the adoption and benefits realisation phases of the extended life cycle, long after the project manager has moved on.

teach.body: In a linear life cycle, most benefits appear after the single transition, so tracking before then relies on forecasts. In an iterative life cycle, increments are released early and often, so some benefits start flowing during the project and can be measured sooner. The backlog is prioritised by value, which keeps benefits at the centre of every time box. Either way, benefits need owners, measures and baselines.

teach.text: Benefits are NOT deliverables and are not scheduled as project milestones. The project delivers outputs; benefits come when outputs are used. And the project manager is not accountable for realising benefits after handover: the SPONSOR is, supported by benefit owners in the business.

teach.h: How this comes up in a written answer
items: Define benefits management: identification, definition, planning, tracking and realisation of benefits.
Explain that a benefit is a measurable improvement from an outcome, valued by stakeholders.
Say what each benefit needs: an owner, a measure, a baseline, a target and timing.
Explain that many benefits come after handover, so tracking continues into BAU.
Give the consequence of skipping it: outputs delivered but no proven or sustained value.
Five activities in order: identification, definition, planning, tracking, realisation.
Benefit: measurable improvement from an outcome, seen as an advantage. Dis-benefit: seen as negative.
Benefits map: outputs → capabilities/outcomes → benefits → strategic objectives.
Each benefit needs an owner, measure, baseline, target and timing.
Most benefits are realised after handover; the sponsor is accountable, with benefit owners.

summary: You can now explain what benefits management is and describe its five activities in order. You can also build a simple benefits map and explain why every benefit needs an owner, measure, baseline, target and timing.

A.q: Which is the correct order of benefits management activities?
options: Define, identify, track, plan, realise
Identify, plan, define, realise, track
Plan, identify, define, track, realise
Identify, define, plan, track, realise
A.why: Benefits management runs identification, definition, planning, tracking and realisation.

whyNot.0: You can't define a benefit before you have identified it.
whyNot.1: Definition comes before planning, and tracking comes before realisation.
whyNot.2: Planning comes after benefits are identified and defined.

options: A benefit that arrives later than planned
A result a stakeholder sees as negative
A benefit claimed by two projects
A benefit that cannot be measured
A.why: A dis-benefit is a measurable result of change that one or more stakeholders perceive as negative.

whyNot.0: A late benefit is still a benefit; it's a timing problem.
whyNot.2: Double counting is a reporting problem, not the meaning of dis-benefit.
whyNot.3: A benefit should always be measurable; that doesn't make it a dis-benefit.

A.q: A bank launches a chatbot to reduce call volumes, but never recorded call volumes before launch. What is the MAIN problem?
options: Nobody can show how far calls have fallen
The chatbot will fail its acceptance tests
The project must restart from Concept
The sponsor cannot approve the budget
A.why: Without a baseline there's no 'before' figure, so the size of the improvement can't be proven.

whyNot.1: Acceptance tests check the output works; they don't depend on a benefits baseline.
whyNot.2: A missing baseline is a measurement problem; it doesn't mean restarting the project.
whyNot.3: Budget approval happened earlier; the issue now is proving the benefit.

B.q: Complete the benefits map: outputs → ___ → benefits → strategic objectives.
options: deliverables
work packages
success factors
outcomes
B.why: Outputs enable capabilities and outcomes, which lead to benefits that contribute to strategic objectives.

whyNot.0: Deliverables are another word for outputs, so they can't sit between outputs and benefits.
whyNot.1: Work packages produce the outputs; they come before outputs, not after.
whyNot.2: Success factors are conditions for success, not a link in the benefits chain.

B.q: Who is normally accountable for benefits being realised after the project closes?
options: The project manager, until all are realised
The sponsor, supported by benefit owners
The team, through the support period
The supplier who built the main outputs
B.why: The sponsor is accountable for benefits, working with benefit owners and users in the business after the project has closed.

whyNot.0: The PM leaves at closure; benefits often take months or years to appear.
whyNot.2: The project team disbands; it doesn't own benefits in BAU.
whyNot.3: Suppliers deliver outputs; the business must use them to realise benefits.

B.q: A hospital's e-prescribing project defines one benefit as 'better medication safety'. What is the MAIN weakness?
options: It has no measure, baseline or target
It is linked to a strategic objective
It is owned by the chief pharmacist
It will be realised after handover
B.why: Definition makes a benefit measurable. 'Better safety' needs a measure (e.g. prescribing errors), a baseline and a target.

whyNot.1: Linking to strategy is a strength, not a weakness.
whyNot.2: A named owner in the business is exactly what a benefit needs.
whyNot.3: Most benefits are realised after handover; that's normal.

C.q: Six months after a new CRM system went live, sales staff still use their old spreadsheets and the forecast revenue gain hasn't appeared. Which activity MOST needs attention now?
options: Identification: find more benefits
Definition: reword the benefit
Realisation: drive adoption
Planning: re-date the milestones
C.why: Tracking has revealed the gap; realisation is about embedding the change (training, process, support) so the outputs are used and the benefit is achieved.

whyNot.0: The benefit is already identified; adding more doesn't fix low adoption.
whyNot.1: The benefit is clear; the problem is that the outputs aren't being used.
whyNot.3: Moving dates doesn't change behaviour; adoption does.

C.q: Which of the following is NOT normally recorded for each benefit?
options: Its named owner
Its baseline value
Its work package
Its target value
C.why: Work packages belong to the WBS and describe project work. A benefit needs an owner, measure, baseline, target and timing.

whyNot.0: An owner is essential so someone is accountable for realising it.
whyNot.1: A baseline gives the 'before' figure to measure improvement against.
whyNot.3: A target states how much improvement is expected.

C.q: Why do many benefits fall within the extended life cycle rather than the project life cycle?
options: They are delivered before outputs are built
They are only checked at the final gate
They are the PM's main project output
They rely on outputs being used over time
C.why: Benefits come from outcomes, which depend on outputs being adopted and used in BAU, so they often appear months after handover.

whyNot.0: Benefits follow outputs; they can't come first.
whyNot.1: Benefits reviews continue after the project; they aren't limited to the final gate.
whyNot.2: The PM delivers outputs; benefits are realised by the business.

reteach.title: Buying a rowing machine
reteach.question: You buy a rowing machine to get fitter. Where are the output, the outcome and the benefit, and what would 'benefits management' look like at home?

blocks.h: Owning it isn't the same as using it
blocks.body: The rowing machine is the output: delivered, assembled, done. The outcome is you rowing three times a week. The benefit is the measurable improvement: resting heart rate down from 78 to 68 in six months. Benefits management means writing down your starting heart rate (baseline), setting a target and a date, deciding who's responsible (you), checking monthly (tracking) and changing habits if it's not working (realisation).

steps.label: Output
steps.sub: Rowing machine in the spare room

blocks.text: A rowing machine used as a clothes horse is a delivered output with zero benefit. Projects fall into the same trap when nobody owns adoption.

explain.body: Identification asks what will be better and for whom (including dis-benefits). Definition turns each benefit into something measurable, with a measure, a baseline and a target.

test.q: During Concept, a project team runs a workshop asking 'what will be better, and for whom, if this succeeds?' Which activity is this?
options: Benefits tracking
Benefits realisation
Benefits identification
Benefits communications
test.why: Working out what improvements the project could bring, and for whom, is benefits identification.

whyNot.0: Tracking measures progress once benefits are defined and planned.
whyNot.1: Realisation embeds the change after delivery.
whyNot.3: Communicating benefits matters, but it isn't one of the five benefits management activities.

explain.body: Planning sets out how and when each benefit will be realised: its owner, timing, the outputs and business changes it depends on, and how it will be measured. It is often captured in a benefits realisation plan and benefit profiles.

test.q: What does benefits planning MAINLY add?
options: How and when each benefit will be realised
The full list of outputs to be handed over
The schedule of the team's work packages
The risks the supplier has agreed to accept
test.why: Planning sets out how, when and by whom each benefit will be realised and measured.

whyNot.1: Outputs are defined in the PBS and scope.
whyNot.2: Work packages are scheduled in the project schedule.
whyNot.3: Supplier risk allocation belongs in the procurement strategy and contract.

explain.body: Tracking measures actual and forecast benefits against targets, during the project and after handover, often through benefits reviews. Its purpose is early warning so corrective action can be taken.

test.q: Benefits tracking shows a forecast saving falling well behind target. What should follow?
options: Remove the benefit from the business case
Wait for the post-project review to act
Close the project down immediately
Agree corrective action with the owner
test.why: Tracking exists to trigger corrective action, agreed with the benefit owner, while there's still time.

whyNot.0: Removing it hides the problem rather than addressing it.
whyNot.1: Waiting wastes the early warning tracking provides.
whyNot.2: Closure may be considered if the case fails, but corrective action comes first.

explain.body: Realisation is when the improvement actually happens. It depends on adoption: people using the outputs and working in the new way. Training, process changes and support make it stick.

test.q: What MOST determines whether a benefit is actually realised?
options: Delivering every output on its planned date
Users adopting and using the outputs
Writing a detailed benefits register
The size of the project's contingency
test.why: Benefits come from outcomes, and outcomes depend on outputs being adopted and used.

whyNot.0: On-time delivery is project success; it doesn't guarantee use.
whyNot.2: A register records benefits; it doesn't realise them.
whyNot.3: Contingency covers risks during delivery; it doesn't create benefits.
